The Nature of Cover Data

Theory, Chapter 1

theory-01-the-nature-of-cover-data.Rmd

What is vegetation cover?

Vegetation cover is a statement about space. When we say that a species has 40% cover in a plot, we mean that 40% of the plot area is occupied by that species. This is not a score, not an index, and not a proxy for something else. It is a direct claim about physical presence in a bounded region.

This definition has consequences. Cover cannot be negative, because a species cannot occupy less than no space. Cover cannot exceed 100%, because a species cannot occupy more space than exists. These are not statistical constraints imposed for convenience. They are logical necessities that follow from what cover means.

The same structure appears in other domains: market shares, budget allocations, time-use data, chemical concentrations in mixtures. In each case, the quantity represents a proportion of a finite whole. The finiteness is not incidental. It defines the quantity.

The three defining constraints

Cover data have three structural properties that any honest treatment must respect.

Boundedness. Cover values live on a closed interval. For a single species, this interval is [0, 1] when expressed as a proportion. A value of 0.4 means something; a value of 1.3 does not. This bound is not a ceiling that data happen to respect. It is a boundary beyond which the quantity ceases to exist.

Compositionality. When multiple species share a plot, their covers are not independent. The total cover across all species must sum to exactly one: the plot is partitioned, and every point in the plot belongs to exactly one category (which may include bare ground or litter as a residual class). If species A occupies 60% of a plot, then all other categories together occupy exactly 40%. This is not a modelling assumption. It is a consequence of measuring area within a finite boundary.

Prevalence of structural zeros. In most vegetation surveys, many species are absent from most plots. These zeros are not missing data, not measurement failures, and not values below some detection threshold. They are exact: the species is not there. This creates a sharp distinction between absence (cover = 0) and presence (cover > 0) that cannot be smoothed away.

These three properties are not independent nuisances. They interact. The bounds constrain the sum. The sum constrains individual values. The zeros are structurally different from small positive values. Any approach that addresses one property while ignoring the others has misunderstood the data.

Why transformation does not help

A common response to bounded data is to transform them onto an unbounded scale, fit a standard model, and back-transform the results. For cover data, this strategy fails at a structural level.

Consider the logit transformation, which maps (0, 1) to the real line. This transformation is undefined at 0 and 1. Since cover data routinely include exact zeros (and sometimes exact ones, for dominant species), the transformation cannot be applied without first modifying the data. Common modifications include adding a small constant, replacing zeros with half the detection limit, or treating zeros as a separate category. Each of these modifications changes what the data say. The zeros are no longer exact. The bounds are no longer hard. The data have been altered to fit the method, rather than the method being chosen to fit the data.

The problem is deeper than undefined values. The logit transformation assumes that the quantity being transformed is a probability or a proportion that could, in principle, take any value in (0, 1). But cover data do not behave this way. A species with 0.1% cover is not “almost absent” in the same sense that a probability of 0.001 is “almost zero”. The species is present. Its cover could increase without bound up to 100%. The geometry near zero is fundamentally different from the geometry near the middle of the interval.

Compositional constraints create additional problems. If species covers must sum to exactly one, then any model that treats their transformed values as independent has imposed an incorrect independence structure. The constraint will be violated in expectation, in variance, or both. Transforming each species separately and hoping the results combine sensibly is not a modelling strategy. It is an evasion.

The structural nature of the failure

These are not approximation errors that become negligible with large samples. They are category errors.

When a model places positive probability on impossible values, it has not made a small mistake. It has described a different quantity than the one measured. Predictions of negative cover or cover exceeding 100% are not merely implausible. They are meaningless. A model that produces them, even occasionally, has failed to represent the data-generating process.

When a model treats exact zeros as inconvenient, it has refused to engage with a central feature of the data. In most vegetation datasets, the zeros carry as much information as the positive values. A species being absent from a plot is not a gap in the data. It is the data.

When a model ignores compositional constraints, it has assumed that species occupy space independently of one another. This is false. Space is finite. What one species occupies, another cannot. This is not a subtle biological interaction that might or might not hold. It is geometry.

What this means for modelling

The constraints of cover data are not obstacles to be overcome. They define the space in which the data exist. Any model for cover data must respect this space, not as a post-hoc correction, but as a foundational commitment.

This does not mean that modelling cover data is impossible, or that no useful work has been done. It means that the starting point matters. A model built on the assumption that cover is an unbounded continuous variable, later constrained through truncation or transformation, begins from a false premise. The constraints will reassert themselves as inconsistencies, boundary effects, and predictions that do not make sense.

The alternative is to begin with the constraints. To treat the bounded, compositional, zero-structured nature of cover as the defining feature of the problem.

This vignette makes no claim about how to do this. It claims only that it must be done.
